source.title: Neural scaling laws and evolution of learnable activation functions of Kolmogorov-Arnold networks
source.authors: T. Čadež; Sanghoon Lee; Kyoung-Min Kim

record.file_problem: The main article text is present and readable. It refers to supplementary notes and tables that are not included in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures scaling curves in KANs and reports broken power laws and task- and architecture-dependent exponents, refining the scope of a single universal scaling form. It does not test language-model pretraining or compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The study measures test loss while varying training dataset size for KAN image-classification and scientific regression tasks. It does not measure language-model loss against parameter count, tokens, or compute; extrapolation from small language-model runs; compute-optimal parameter/token allocation; or downstream language-task performance. Edge-function analyses are not rows because they do not measure the scaling behavior in the claim.
record.test_reason: The study measures test loss against training-set size for three KAN variants on image classification and scientific regression. It reports broken power laws in classification and exponents that depend on architecture and task, and argues against universal exponents. This bears on V5 (power-law form in other modalities) and V7 (curves bend; exponents depend on setup). It does not study language models, parameter or compute scaling laws, or compute-optimal allocation.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors find broken neural scaling laws in KAN test loss against dataset size. Classification passes through random-guess, faster- and slower-scaling regimes; regression crosses from random-guess to a single power law with exponents near 2. Exponents depend strongly on KAN implementation and task, which they contrast with claims of universal exponents. They argue for case-by-case analysis, and suggest the high exponents mean KANs scale well.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures test loss for KANs on image classification and scientific regression while varying dataset size. It does not use language models or measure parameter-, token-, or compute-scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported scaling behavior varies with KAN architecture, task, dataset, and hidden-neuron count. The text says regression results are robust to edge-function hyperparameters; learning-rate scheme has a minor but variant-dependent effect, and increasing training epochs can lower some wider-model losses.

fits_no_version.finding: Gottlieb-KAN edge functions keep one shape family (effective rank about 1) as the dataset grows, while loss falls by orders of magnitude.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss improvement with data in KANs comes from rescaling edge functions, not from more diverse function shapes.

fits_no_version.finding: KAN regression exponents (1.28–2.59) are higher than MLP exponents (0.82–2.29, cited from Ref. 9) and, unlike the MLP ones, do not grow with model size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data-scaling exponents depend on network family: KANs versus MLPs.

record.problems: The study uses non-language KANs and varies dataset size rather than language-model parameters, tokens, or compute. Many per-width fit values and uncertainty estimates are only referenced in supplementary material not supplied here; the regression discussion notes larger deviations and error bars for Gottlieb-KAN.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports additional per-width fitted values in Figures 3 and 5 and additional curve values in Figures 2, 4, and 7; these were not extracted individually because the supplied text does not state their exact values. Edge-function shape and effective-rank measurements were omitted because they do not measure the scaling behaviors in the claim.

untested.parts: All of it: language-model pretraining loss against parameters, tokens or compute.
All of it: no extrapolation from small to large runs.
All of it: no compute-optimal allocation.
Depth and width at a fixed parameter count. Width is varied, but parameter count changes with it.
Scaling in parameters or compute (only dataset size is varied), video models, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer.
All of it: no downstream tasks.
Parameter-counting conventions, comparison of fitting methods, and the disagreement between published language-model laws.

missing.what: Overall classification exponent ranges across variants and widths: α 0.4–1.5, β 0.06–0.6.
The MLP baseline shows a single power law over the measured range in both task types, with no random-guess plateau or FS-to-SS break.
missing.locator: Section II A 1 and II B 1; Supplementary Notes 1–2

missing.what: Regression loss gains from width largely saturate by nh=16 (models of 31,481–5,225,280 parameters). Loss is therefore not a power law in model size here.

Robustness checks: regression results are robust to edge-function hyperparameters; the learning-rate scheme has a minor, variant-dependent effect; the fixed epoch budget makes wider models underperform at small N_D until more epochs are used.

record.verdict_notes: This is a non-language setting that varies only dataset size, so V5 and V7 are the only versions it bears on. Regression rows were marked partial in the record; they are fixed to observed because the LS regime is a clean single power law. Rows r17–r19 pool all three variants but are labelled BSRBF-KAN. Rows r11–r16 have duplicated value text. The α=1.73 in r20 conflicts with the Fig. 8 θ range. Per-width fits and their uncertainties sit in supplementary tables that were not supplied.

Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation, and how either scales with compute.
Depth, width, and other architecture changes at fixed parameter count.
Video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, transfer, and whether the same law holds in language-model training regimes.
Predictability of downstream language-task performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Language-model setup and fitting choices, parameter-counting conventions, compute-optimal allocation, and whether published language-model laws disagree.

rows.measure: Test cross-entropy loss versus training dataset size; fitted faster- and slower-scaling exponents and crossover.
rows.value: The fit gives α = 0.50, β = 0.11, and N× = 9.3 × 10³; the curve passes from a small-data random-guess regime through faster scaling and then slower scaling.
rows.note: The reported result is a broken scaling curve, not one power law across the full dataset-size range.
rows.check: For V5, a power law holds only within finite windows: two exponents (α=0.50, β=0.11) with a crossover. Split the versions: for V7 the state is observed, since the curve bends from one power law to another.
